passage:
Mentor meeting note, Tuesday. Divyansh, third year.
Divyansh was quiet today. When I asked about his week, he said he'd been scrolling back through his chat with Mohit, his school friend from Indore, and realised their last proper conversation was in February. It is September now. "We didn't fight or anything," he said. "Nothing happened. That's what's weird. I can't even be angry at anyone."
He said he feels silly being sad about "basically nothing" when other people have real problems. He kept clicking his pen cap on and off.
I told him that a friendship slowly going quiet is still a loss, and it is all right to feel sad about it without a big reason. He looked surprised at that, then a little relieved.
I suggested he could write to Mohit if he wanted, or simply let himself miss him for now. Will check in next week.

qa.q: When was Divyansh's last proper conversation with Mohit?
qa.a: Their last proper conversation was in February.

qa.q: Why does Divyansh feel silly for being sad?
qa.a: Divyansh thinks the sadness has no real cause, since nothing happened and there was no fight, so it feels like being sad about 'basically nothing'.

qa.q: How did the mentor help Divyansh at this stage?
qa.a: The mentor named the fading as a real loss, gave Divyansh permission to feel sad, and offered choices: write to Mohit or simply miss him for now.

qa.q: How might Mohit be experiencing these same months?
qa.a: Mohit may not have noticed the gap at all, or may feel the same quiet sadness without saying it, since there was never any fight.

grounding: Shows a young man realising months have passed since a real talk with his school friend and feeling sad with nothing to blame, and a mentor allowing that grief.

passage:
Sunday night
Santosh posted a photo today from a trek. With people I don't know. And it hit me: I didn't know he'd gone. I didn't even know he liked trekking now.
I scrolled up our chat. Last real message: 12 May, about my cousin's wedding. After that, just birthday wishes and one forwarded joke. Four months.
We didn't fight. Nobody left. There's nothing I can point to and say, that's when. That makes it worse somehow, because who do I tell? "My friend is fine and we just stopped talking"? Sounds like nothing.
But it doesn't feel like nothing. It feels like when Nani's house was sold. Same rooms, just not ours any more.
Maybe I'm allowed to be sad about this. I think I am.
Lalit

qa.q: What was the last real message in the chat about?
qa.a: The last real message was about Lalit's cousin's wedding, on 12 May.

qa.q: Why does the lack of a fight make Lalit feel worse?
qa.a: With nothing to point to, Lalit feels no one would accept it as a reason to be sad, so the hurt has nowhere to go.

qa.q: What could Lalit do next with this sadness?
qa.a: Lalit could let the grief be real, talk about it with someone close, and decide whether to message Santosh about the trek to see what is still worth keeping.

qa.q: How might Santosh see the last four months?
qa.a: Santosh has probably just been busy with new people and trekking and may not see the silence as an ending at all.

grounding: Illustrates quiet grief when a friendship fades with no single event to blame, a loss that feels hard to mourn openly.

passage:
Emil was scrolling back through his messages on the tram in Copenhagen, looking for a restaurant address, when he reached Oskar's name and stopped.

The last real message was from March. Oskar had written three long paragraphs about his breakup, and Emil had replied, "That's rough, let's talk this weekend." They hadn't. After that there were only birthday wishes and a thumbs up on a photo.

It was October now.

There had been no fight. No moment he could point to. They had lived in the same corridor for three years at university; Oskar had driven him to the hospital the night he broke his wrist.

Emil put the phone in his pocket and looked out at the grey harbour. He felt something close to grief, and then felt a bit silly for it. Nobody had died. Nobody had even left. It had just... faded.

qa.q: When was the last real message between Emil and Oskar?
qa.a: March.

qa.q: Why does Emil feel silly about feeling close to grief?
qa.a: He feels sad about losing Oskar but also feels he has no right to mourn, since nobody died or left and there was no single event to blame.

qa.q: What could Emil do with this sadness?
qa.a: He could let himself feel it as a real loss, and if he wants, send Oskar a message about a specific memory to see if the friendship can be revived.

qa.q: How might Oskar remember the unanswered "let's talk this weekend"?
qa.a: He may have felt a little let down after sharing his breakup, and quietly drifted too, perhaps also sad without knowing why.

grounding: Emil realises months have passed since a real talk with Oskar and feels a quiet grief with no single cause, and a sense he has no permission to mourn it.

passage:
The college library in Pune was almost empty during the holidays. Sudha had come to return a book and found herself sitting at the table by the window, the one where she and Omkar had spent all of second year.

Their initials were still scratched faintly under the edge. S + O, study partners, not the other thing, they used to joke.

She tried to remember the last time they had actually talked. Not a "congrats!!" under a post, but talked. It must have been before his internship, before her exams. Eight months, maybe nine.

Nothing had happened. They hadn't fought. It was just that each week had been busy, and then it had been a year.

Sudha sat there longer than she meant to. When the librarian began switching off the lights, her eyes were wet, and she didn't quite know how to explain why.

qa.q: What was scratched faintly under the edge of the table?
qa.a: Their initials, S + O.

qa.q: How can you tell Sudha feels sad about the friendship?
qa.a: She sits longer than she meant to and her eyes are wet, feeling sad and a little lost, though she cannot explain why since nothing happened.

qa.q: What small step might help Sudha now?
qa.a: She could accept that the sadness is real and, if she wants the friendship back, message Omkar about the window table and ask to talk.

qa.q: How might Omkar see these eight or nine months?
qa.a: He may also have been caught in busy weeks during his internship and not noticed the fading, or noticed and felt sad in the same quiet way.

grounding: Sudha, sitting at an old library table, realises months have passed since a real talk with Omkar and feels an unexplained grief for a friendship that faded without any event.

passage:
Sabina,

I'm not sure I'll send this.

I was clearing my phone last night and found our old voice notes from first year, the ones where we narrated each other's bad days like cricket commentary. I laughed out loud, alone in my room, and then I didn't feel like laughing.

I tried to remember our last real conversation. I think it was when your grandmother was unwell, in February. Since then, it's been hearts on photos and "we should catch up!!" that neither of us followed through.

Nothing went wrong. I keep looking for the moment, and there isn't one. That's the part that's hard to explain to anyone. You can't say "I lost a friend" when nobody left.

But it feels like I did.

Nitin

qa.q: What did Nitin find while clearing the phone?
qa.a: Their old voice notes from first year.

qa.q: What is Nitin feeling after the laughter stops?
qa.a: Nitin feels sad and a quiet grief, missing Sabina, while also struggling because there was no moment of loss to point to.

qa.q: What could Nitin do with this letter?
qa.a: Nitin could send it, or a shorter version, since naming the loss honestly might reopen the friendship, or at least let Nitin mourn it properly.

qa.q: What might Sabina feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Sabina might be surprised and moved, perhaps sad too, and relieved to know the fading hurt Nitin as well.

grounding: Nitin's unsent letter shows the sadness of realising a friendship with Sabina has faded with no single event to blame, a loss that feels hard to mourn.

passage:
You asked why I looked sad scrolling through my phone. Okay. I'm Mahima, and I just realised something stupid.

Vinita and I were inseparable in first year. Every exam, every heartbreak, every terrible mess dinner. Then she moved to the other campus for her specialisation. We said we'd meet every Sunday.

I scrolled up just now. Our last real conversation was in March. It's October. Since then? Birthday wishes. A few hearts. One "we should catch up!!" that neither of us followed up.

Nothing happened. No fight. Nobody did anything wrong. That's what makes it strange. If we'd fought, I'd know what to be sad about.

But I am sad. It feels like losing someone, and I don't think I'm allowed to call it that, because she's still right there on my phone.

qa.q: When was Mahima's last real conversation with Vinita?
qa.a: It was in March.

qa.q: What is Mahima feeling after scrolling through the chat?
qa.a: Mahima feels a quiet sadness and grief, like a loss, but unsure it's allowed since there was no fight.

qa.q: What could Mahima do with this feeling?
qa.a: Mahima could let the sadness be real, and if the friendship still matters, send Vinita a specific message suggesting a time to talk.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel if she noticed the same gap?
qa.a: Vinita might feel the same quiet sadness and guilt, perhaps waiting for Mahima to reach out first.

grounding: A spoken account shows someone realising months have passed without a real talk and grieving a friendship that faded with no single cause.
